title: Void Bets in Canada: Sportsbook Settlement Rules Explained
excerpt: Void bets, dead heats and postponements decide more wagers than Canadians expect. Here is how sportsbook settlement rules actually work, and when to argue.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Most Canadian bettors learn the settlement rules the hard way. A starting pitcher is scratched an hour before first pitch and a total disappears from the bet slip. A tennis player retires in the second set and a comfortable winner turns into a refund. Two golfers finish level and a payout arrives at half the expected size. Void bets and unusual settlements decide more wagers over a season than most people realise, and almost none of it is arbitrary — it is written down in a rules document that nobody reads until something goes wrong.

This guide explains how sportsbook settlement rules work in Canada, which situations differ meaningfully between books, and how to tell a genuine error from a correct outcome you simply did not expect.

What a void actually means

A void — sometimes called a push, a no action or a cancelled bet depending on the context — means the wager is treated as though it never happened. Your stake returns to your balance and nothing is won or lost. In a parlay, a voided leg typically drops out and the remaining legs recalculate at their combined odds, so a four-leg parlay with one void becomes a three-leg parlay rather than a loss.

That last mechanic matters more than it sounds, because it changes the payout without changing the number of bets you thought you had. Bettors who build parlays around a specific expected return are often surprised by a smaller payout that is entirely correct under the rules.

The situations that trigger a void

Books differ in the details, but the common triggers are broadly consistent across the licensed Canadian market.

  • Event postponed or abandoned. Most books void if a game is not completed within a defined window — often 24 to 72 hours from the original start — though some sports carry their own conventions.
  • Player does not participate. Player props almost universally void if the athlete takes no part in the game. Whether a brief appearance counts is where books diverge.
  • Listed pitcher rules. In baseball, bets taken with designated starting pitchers void if a listed starter does not begin the game, unless you opted into action-regardless pricing.
  • Retirement or walkover. Tennis is the classic case, and rules vary sharply: some books settle once a set is complete, others require the full match.
  • Obvious pricing error. Books reserve the right to void bets taken at a palpably wrong price, and every licensed operator has such a clause.
  • Venue or format change. A neutral-site relocation or a change in match length can void wagers where the change materially alters the proposition.

Dead heats: the rule that surprises everyone

A dead heat occurs when two or more selections tie for a position that only one was supposed to occupy — two golfers sharing third place in a top-five market, two players tying for most goals, two horses finishing level. Rather than voiding, books apply dead heat reduction: your stake is divided by the number of participants tying for the places available, and the bet is settled on that reduced portion at full odds.

The practical effect is a payout well below what the displayed odds implied, and it is entirely legitimate. Golf outright and finishing-position markets produce dead heats regularly, and bettors who play those markets should understand the mechanic before it costs them. If you are still building your foundation in how odds translate to returns, our guide to the basics of sports betting covers the arithmetic in plain terms.

Where books genuinely differ

Some settlement questions have no universal answer, and this is where reading a specific book's rules pays for itself.

Overtime inclusion

Whether a market includes overtime is a house rule, not a law of nature. Team totals and most player props generally include it, but certain markets in certain sports do not, and a bettor who assumes wrongly can watch a winning position settle as a loss.

Minimum play requirements

For an abandoned game, one book might require a full regulation period while another settles markets already determined. In baseball, the length of play needed for a game to be considered official for betting purposes is defined in the rules and does not always match the league's own definition.

Related contingencies in same-game parlays

When one leg of a same-game parlay voids, the correlation that made the parlay attractive disappears. Books handle the recalculation differently, and some will void the entire bet rather than reprice it.

Cash-out and void interaction

If you cash out a bet and the event is later voided, the cash-out generally stands — the transaction was completed. Bettors sometimes expect a refund on top, and that is not how it works.

How to check the rules before you need them

Every licensed Canadian sportsbook publishes its rules, usually as a sport-by-sport document linked from the footer or the help centre. It is dry reading, but you only need to look at the sports you actually bet and the specific markets you use. Ten minutes spent on the tennis and baseball sections will spare you the two most common settlement surprises in the Canadian market.

Pay particular attention to any section headed maximum payout, which caps what the book will pay on a single wager regardless of the odds. This rarely affects ordinary bets but can significantly change a large longshot parlay, and it is enforceable because it was disclosed. Differences like these are part of what we weigh across our operator coverage, including our Campeonbet sportsbook review.

When a settlement is actually wrong

Errors do happen. A market settles on the wrong result, a void is applied where the rules do not call for one, or a statistical correction from the league is not reflected. The process for challenging it is straightforward and works far better when you are calm and specific.

Screenshot your bet slip as soon as you notice a problem. Identify the exact rule you believe applies and quote it back — settlement teams respond to rule citations far more constructively than to general complaints. Note the official data source the book uses, since many sports markets are settled on league-supplied feeds and a discrepancy with a third-party stats site is not evidence of an error. Then open a support ticket rather than a live chat if the issue needs investigation, because a ticket creates a written record.

If the operator's internal process does not resolve it and you are in a regulated province, there is a complaints path beyond the sportsbook itself. That escalation route is one of the genuine advantages of betting with a licensed operator, and it is a reason we point Ontario bettors toward the provincially licensed books listed on our Ontario sports betting guide.

The habit that prevents most disputes

Nearly every settlement argument traces back to a bettor assuming a rule rather than checking one. Before you place a wager in an unfamiliar market — a player prop in a sport you do not usually bet, a finishing-position market, anything involving a tournament format — take a moment to confirm how it settles and what voids it. If you are shopping across several operators, and you should be, remember that the rules travel with the book rather than the market, so the same bet at two sites can settle differently.

Compare your options across the licensed Canadian market through our sportsbook rankings, and read the rules once for each book you use. It is a tedious afternoon that quietly pays for itself over a season.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
